Post-Incident Report: Checkout payment failures
Prepared by: Site Reliability, Kestrel Home Goods (online store)
Incident window: Saturday 12 September 2026, 10:42am to 1:17pm AEST
Severity: 2

Summary
For about two and a half hours on Saturday morning, a share of card payments at checkout failed with a generic "payment could not be processed" error. The problem was caused by an expired intermediate certificate on one of our two payment gateway connectors. Traffic was load balanced across both connectors, so roughly half of payment attempts were affected.

Impact
During the window, 4,812 checkout attempts were made. Of these, 2,391 failed. Our analysis of customer sessions shows that 1,940 of the customers who hit a failure retried and completed their purchase, either straight away or later that day. The remaining 451 did not complete a purchase on Saturday. Based on average order value, those 451 abandoned orders represent an estimated $41,900 in lost revenue, although some of these customers may have bought later in the week.

Customer support received 312 contacts about payment failures, which was about four times the normal Saturday volume.

Timeline
10:42 - First failed payments logged. Alerting threshold not met because failures were spread across both connectors' metrics.
11:35 - Support team escalated after a spike in chat contacts.
12:10 - On-call engineer identified certificate expiry on connector B.
12:58 - Connector B removed from rotation.
1:17 - Failure rate back to normal baseline.

Root cause
The certificate was renewed by the vendor in August, but our connector B config pinned the old intermediate certificate. Connector A had been updated in an earlier change and was unaffected.

Actions
1. Remove certificate pinning from both connectors (Owner: Platform team, due 30 September) - done.
2. Add an alert on overall checkout failure rate, not just per connector (Owner: SRE, due 17 October).
3. Add certificate expiry to the monthly vendor dependency check (Owner: Security, due 31 October).
4. Send a goodwill 10 per cent discount code to customers who hit a failure and did not purchase (Owner: Marketing, due 20 September) - sent.
reference: Key points: Saturday 12 Sept, about 2.5 hours of payment failures caused by an expired/pinned intermediate certificate on connector B; 2,391 of 4,812 attempts failed but most retried; 451 customers did not complete, about $41,900 estimated lost revenue; detection was slow (support escalated after nearly an hour and the cause was found about 1.5 hours in) because alerting was per connector, so the overall failure rate was not alerted on; open actions: overall failure-rate alert (SRE, 17 Oct) and certificate expiry checks (Security, 31 Oct). TRAP: several similar numbers - 2,391 failed attempts vs 451 lost customers vs 1,940 recovered; saying 2,391 lost sales or attaching $41,900 to the wrong figure is wrong.

Policy Update: Paid Parental Leave
Effective: 1 January 2027
Issued by: People and Culture, Tallowood Health Network

What's changing

From 1 January 2027, Tallowood will increase employer-paid parental leave for primary carers from 12 weeks to 18 weeks at full pay. Secondary carer leave will increase from 2 weeks to 4 weeks at full pay. Both entitlements are in addition to the government Parental Leave Pay scheme.

We are also removing the requirement that leave be taken in a single block. Primary carers will be able to split their 18 weeks into up to three blocks, as long as all leave is taken within 24 months of the birth or adoption.

Who is eligible

The increased entitlements apply to employees whose child is born or placed for adoption on or after 1 January 2027. Employees whose child arrives before that date remain on the current entitlements (12 weeks and 2 weeks), even if part of their leave falls after 1 January.

To be eligible, employees must have completed 12 months of continuous service by the expected date of birth or placement. Casual employees are eligible if they have worked on a regular and systematic basis for at least 12 months.

Superannuation

Tallowood will continue to pay superannuation on the employer-paid portion of leave. We will also now pay superannuation on the government-funded portion for primary carers, up to 18 weeks.

How to apply

Submit the parental leave form through the staff portal at least 10 weeks before the expected start of leave. Your manager will receive an automatic notification. If your circumstances change, for example because of an early birth, let your manager and People and Culture know as soon as possible and we will adjust the dates.

Questions

The People and Culture team will hold two online information sessions on 5 November and 19 November at 12:30pm. Recordings will be posted on the intranet. You can also contact parentalleave@tallowood.example.org.au.

We know a lot of staff have been asking for this change, and we'd like to thank the Staff Wellbeing Committee for their work on the proposal.
reference: Key points: primary carer leave rises from 12 to 18 weeks full pay, secondary from 2 to 4 weeks; leave can be split into up to three blocks within 24 months; super now also paid on the government-funded portion (primary carers, up to 18 weeks); 12 months service required, regular casuals eligible; apply 10 weeks ahead. TRAP: the new entitlements apply only where the child is born or placed on or after 1 January 2027 - a summary implying anyone on leave after 1 January gets 18 weeks, or omitting the condition, is wrong.

Research Brief: Sit-Stand Desks and Afternoon Productivity
Centre for Workplace Health, University of Coastal Queensland (fictional study, internal brief)

Background
Sit-stand desks are now common in Australian offices, and suppliers often claim they lift productivity. We wanted to test whether access to a sit-stand desk changes measurable work output in the afternoon, when self-reported fatigue tends to peak.

Method
We recruited 214 office workers from four organisations in Brisbane and the Gold Coast. Half were randomly given a sit-stand desk for 12 weeks; the other half kept their usual fixed desk. All participants completed a standard 10-minute typing and proofreading task at 3pm twice a week, and wore a sensor that recorded time spent standing.

Findings
On average, the sit-stand group stood for 47 minutes more per working day than the control group in week 2, but this fell to 19 minutes more by week 12.

There was no statistically significant difference between the groups in task speed or accuracy at any point in the study. The difference in accuracy at week 12 was 0.4 percentage points, well inside the margin of error.

The sit-stand group did report lower lower-back discomfort: 31 per cent reported weekly discomfort at week 12, compared with 44 per cent of the control group.

Participant views
Feedback was strongly positive. One participant said, "I've never been so productive in my life, I fly through the afternoons now." Another said the desk "made the 3pm slump disappear". Overall, 78 per cent of the sit-stand group said they felt more productive.

Interpretation
Participants clearly felt more productive, but we did not find any change in measured output. The most reliable benefit was reduced back discomfort. The drop in standing time over 12 weeks also suggests that the novelty wears off, so organisations should not assume desks will be used as heavily in the long run.

Limitations
The task was short and may not reflect real work. Participants could not be blinded to which desk they had.

Funding
This study was funded by a university grant. No desk suppliers were involved.
reference: Key points: 214 workers, randomised, 12 weeks; no measurable difference in task speed or accuracy; sit-stand group had less back discomfort (31% vs 44%); extra standing time fell from 47 to 19 minutes a day as novelty wore off; caveat that the task was short. TRAP: participant quotes and the 78% who felt more productive are opinions, not findings - a summary saying the desks improved productivity is wrong.

Narrawin Aquatic Centre reopens after $3.2 million upgrade

The Narrawin Aquatic Centre will reopen to the public on Saturday 31 October after an eight-month renovation, Greendale Regional Council announced this week.

The upgrade, jointly funded by council and a state government community facilities grant, includes a new heated 25-metre program pool, accessible change rooms with an adult change table, a ramp entry to the main 50-metre pool and a solar array on the grandstand roof that is expected to cover about a third of the centre's power needs.

Mayor Gwen Patterson said the centre had been "well overdue" for a refresh. "The old program pool was nearly fifty years old and was leaking thousands of litres a week," she said. "This means families, older residents and people with disability can all use the centre comfortably, and the heated pool means swim lessons can run all year."

The centre manager, Luke Ambrose, said swim school enrolments for term one would open online on 20 October. Lap swimming, aqua aerobics and the learn-to-swim program will resume from opening day. The outdoor water play area will reopen at the same time.

Entry prices will stay the same as before the closure for the rest of the 2026-27 season: $6.50 for adults, $4.50 for children and concession holders, and free for children under three.

The opening day will include free entry from 10am to 4pm, a sausage sizzle run by the Narrawin Football Club juniors, and a demonstration by the local surf life saving club.

Long-time swimmer Margaret Yeo, 81, said she had missed her morning laps. "I've been driving to Pellham twice a week, which is forty minutes each way. I'll be at the gate at six on the first day."

The centre will open from 6am to 8pm on weekdays and 7am to 6pm on weekends.

More information is on the council website.
reference: Key points: Narrawin Aquatic Centre reopens Saturday 31 October after an eight-month, $3.2 million upgrade; new heated 25m program pool, accessible change rooms, ramp entry, solar on the grandstand; swim school enrolments open 20 October; prices unchanged for the 2026-27 season; free entry on opening day 10am-4pm. No trap. Quotes and sausage sizzle are colour.

Your lease explained: Clause 7 - Rent Review
Prepared for tenants of Bayview Arcade, Shop 14 (plain-English guide, not legal advice)

This guide explains how your rent can change during your five-year lease. Please read it with the full lease, which is the binding document.

What the clause says

Your starting rent is $62,400 a year plus GST, paid monthly. The rent is reviewed on each anniversary of the lease start date (1 March).

In years 2, 3 and 4, the rent goes up by the change in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for Sydney over the previous 12 months. However, the increase is capped. It will be no less than 3 per cent and no more than 5 per cent in any of those years. So if CPI is 2 per cent, your rent still goes up 3 per cent. If CPI is 6 per cent, your rent goes up 5 per cent.

Year 5 is different. In year 5, the rent is reviewed to market. This means the landlord gets a valuer to assess what similar shops in the area are renting for, and your rent is set at that level. The 5 per cent cap does not apply to the market review, and the rent can go up by more. Under clause 7.6, the market review cannot reduce the rent below what you were paying in year 4.

If you disagree with the market valuation, you can ask for an independent valuer within 30 days of receiving the landlord's notice. The cost of the independent valuer is split equally between you and the landlord.

Other things to know

- Outgoings (council rates, strata levies, cleaning of common areas) are charged separately and are not part of the rent review.
- The landlord must give you written notice of each new rent at least 14 days before it starts.
- If the landlord is late with notice, you keep paying the old rent until notice is given, and then pay any difference.

Questions about this guide can go to the centre management office on Level 1.
reference: Key points: five-year lease at $62,400 a year plus GST; years 2-4 rise by Sydney CPI with a floor of 3% and cap of 5%; year 5 is a market review with no cap and can't go below year 4 rent; 30 days to request an independent valuer, cost split; outgoings separate; 14 days notice of new rent. TRAP: the cap applies only in years 2-4 - a summary saying increases are capped at 5% for the whole lease (or that rent can fall in year 5) is wrong. Also the 3% floor means rent rises even when CPI is low.

Tallis Valley Hospital parking fee changes spark concern

Patients and visitors at Tallis Valley Hospital will pay more to park from next month after the health service confirmed changes to its car park fees.

Under the new structure, which starts on 1 November, the first hour will remain free. After that, the hourly rate rises from $3 to $4, and the daily maximum rises from $18 to $24.

However, the health service has also extended concession parking. From 1 November, frequent visitors such as patients having chemotherapy or dialysis, and carers of patients staying more than seven days, can apply for a weekly pass costing $15. The current concession is a daily rate of $9.

The health service's chief operating officer, Rhonda McAllister, said the changes were needed to fund repairs to the multi-level car park, which was built in 1994. "The car park has concrete cancer in two levels and we have had to close 180 spaces," she said. "This is about making it safe, not making a profit."

Local resident Barry Sutton, whose wife has dialysis three times a week, said he had expected the worst. "When I heard the fees were going up I thought we'd be paying a fortune," he said. "But if the weekly pass is real, we'll be paying less than we do now."

Nurses' union delegate Jessica Ward said staff were not affected by the changes, because staff parking is in a separate area and covered by an existing agreement.

Some community members have questioned whether the hospital should charge for parking at all. A petition calling for free parking at regional hospitals has collected more than 2,000 signatures.

The health service said the concession pass application form would be available at the main reception and on its website from 20 October. Patients need a letter from their treating team to apply.

Repairs to the car park are expected to take 18 months, with the closed levels to reopen in stages.
reference: Key points: from 1 November the first hour stays free, hourly rate rises $3 to $4, daily max $18 to $24; new $15 weekly concession pass for frequent visitors (e.g. chemo, dialysis, long-stay carers), compared with the current $9 daily concession; money funds repairs to the car park (180 spaces closed, about 18 months); staff unaffected; pass forms from 20 October, need a treating-team letter. TRAP: the headline suggests everyone pays more, but frequent visitors will likely pay less; a summary that says only "fees go up" misses the main nuance. Several similar dollar figures ($9, $15, $18, $24) are easy to swap.

Incident Report: Positive Legionella sample, Building C cooling tower
Facilities Management, Riverside Business Park
Report date: 9 October 2026
Prepared by: Nathan Cole, Facilities Manager

What happened
Routine monthly water sampling from the Building C cooling tower on 29 September returned a Legionella count of 1,200 CFU/mL. Results were received from the laboratory on 3 October. Under state regulations, a count of 1,000 CFU/mL or more requires notification to the health department within 24 hours, immediate disinfection and resampling.

Response
- 3 October, 2:15pm: Results received. Water treatment contractor called out.
- 3 October, 4:40pm: Health department notified (within the 24-hour requirement).
- 3 October, 6:00pm: Tower shut down and online disinfection started.
- 4 October: Tower drained, cleaned and refilled.
- 6 October: Resample taken.
- 9 October: Resample result: not detected.

The tower has been returned to service. Building C tenants were informed by email on 4 October. No cases of illness linked to the site have been reported to us or to the health department.

Cause
The contractor's assessment is that the biocide dosing pump failed in mid-September and was not picked up because the monthly service visit was missed. The contractor's technician was on leave and no replacement was sent. We were not told the visit had been missed.

Actions
1. Contractor has replaced the dosing pump (complete).
2. Contractor to provide written confirmation of each monthly visit within 48 hours, and notify us immediately if a visit is missed (from November).
3. Facilities to install a dosing pump alarm that alerts the building management system (quoted at $4,800, awaiting approval).
4. Increase sampling to fortnightly for the next three months.

Cost
Disinfection, cleaning and extra testing: $7,350. We are seeking to recover this from the contractor under the service agreement, as the missed visit was a breach.

Approval needed
Action 3 requires approval of $4,800 by the property manager. Until the alarm is installed, Facilities will check the dosing pump manually each week.
reference: Key points: Building C cooling tower sample showed Legionella at 1,200 CFU/mL (above the 1,000 notification level); health department notified on time, tower disinfected, resample clear and back in service; no illness reported; cause was a failed dosing pump missed because the contractor skipped a monthly visit; $7,350 cost being sought from the contractor; fortnightly sampling for three months. TRAP: a $4,800 alarm still needs the property manager's approval - this is the one decision for the manager and is easily dropped or reported as already installed.

Study write-up: Napping on night shift and next-day driving performance
Southern Transport Safety Institute (fictional), summary for member organisations

Why we did this study
Many night-shift workers drive home after their shift. Some workplaces allow a short nap during the break. We wanted to know whether a 20-minute nap during a night shift improves driving performance on the way home.

What we did
We worked with 96 night-shift workers from three distribution centres in Adelaide and Geelong. Each person completed two night shifts in our sleep lab, one with a 20-minute nap at 3am and one without. The order was randomised. After each shift, they completed a 30-minute driving simulator task that measured lane drifting and reaction time.

What we found
After the shift with a nap, lane drifting events fell by 22 per cent compared with the shift without a nap. Average reaction time improved by 0.09 seconds.

But the benefit was not the same for everyone. Workers who had already been on night shift for more than six months got most of the benefit. In workers who were new to night shift (under three months), the nap made no measurable difference to lane drifting, and some reported feeling groggier for the first 15 minutes after waking.

We also found that the effect of the nap was smaller than the effect of the time of the drive. Drives starting at 7am showed about twice as many lane drifting events as drives starting at 6am, with or without a nap.

What this means
A short nap during the night shift is a low-cost measure that can help experienced night workers. It should not be treated as a replacement for other measures, such as rostering so shifts end earlier, or offering transport home after long shift runs.

Limitations
Simulator driving is not the same as real driving. The sample was mostly men aged 25 to 50.

Contact
Dr Leila Hartmann, Program Lead, Fatigue Research.
reference: Key points: 96 night workers, randomised crossover; a 20-minute 3am nap cut lane drifting by 22% and improved reaction time slightly; benefit was mainly in workers with over six months on nights - no measurable difference in lane drifting for workers new to nights (under three months), some of whom felt groggier after waking; finishing time mattered more (7am drives had about twice the drift events of 6am drives); naps complement, not replace, roster changes. TRAP: summarising as "naps make night workers safer drivers" without the experience condition is wrong, and missing that drive timing had a bigger effect understates the key finding.

Your lease explained: Clause 14 - Assignment and Subletting
Unit 6, Kurralta Business Park (plain-English guide for the tenant, Brightside Physio Pty Ltd)

This guide summarises clause 14 of your lease. It is a guide only and the lease itself governs.

The short version
You cannot transfer the lease (assignment) or let someone else use part of the premises (subletting) without the landlord's written consent.

Assignment
If you sell your business and want the buyer to take over the lease, you must ask the landlord in writing. The landlord can't refuse unreasonably, but can ask for:
- financial information about the buyer, such as two years of accounts
- a bank guarantee from the buyer equal to three months' rent
- payment of the landlord's reasonable legal costs, usually between $1,500 and $3,000

Important: even after an assignment, you (and any guarantor) can remain liable for the rent if the new tenant defaults. Under the retail leases legislation in this state, this liability ends 12 months after the assignment, but only if the lease is a retail lease. Your lease is not a retail lease because your business provides health services and the premises are over 1,000 square metres. That means the 12-month release does not apply, and you could remain liable for the rest of the term unless the landlord agrees in writing to release you.

Subletting
You may sublet up to 30 per cent of the floor area (for example, to a massage therapist or dietitian) with the landlord's consent, which can't be unreasonably withheld. Any sublease must be shorter than your own lease and must not allow the subtenant to make structural changes.

Change of control
If the shareholders of Brightside Physio Pty Ltd change so that a new person controls the company, this is treated as an assignment and needs consent.

Practical tips
- Ask for consent early. The landlord has 28 days to respond.
- If you are planning to sell, talk to a lawyer about negotiating a release before the sale.

Contact the landlord's agent, Kingsley Property Group, for consent forms.
reference: Key points: assignment or subletting needs the landlord's written consent (not unreasonably withheld); landlord may require buyer financials, a three-month-rent bank guarantee and $1,500-$3,000 legal costs; subletting allowed up to 30% of floor area; a change in company control counts as an assignment; landlord has 28 days to respond. TRAP: the 12-month release from liability after assignment does NOT apply because this is not a retail lease - Brightside could stay liable for the rest of the term unless released in writing. A summary saying liability ends after 12 months is wrong.

Post-Incident Report: Suspected data breach, customer statements
Coastline Credit Union (fictional) - Information Security
Date: 7 October 2026

Summary
On Friday 2 October, several members reported receiving another member's monthly statement by email. The issue was initially treated as a possible cyber attack. Our investigation found no evidence of external access. The cause was an error in a scheduled job that sends statements.

Initial response
The first member call came in at 8:20am. By 9am the contact centre had 14 similar calls. The duty manager, Craig Daley, escalated to Information Security, and in an all-staff message said: "It looks like we've been hacked. Please do not open any unusual emails." This message was forwarded outside the organisation by at least one staff member and was quoted in a local news story that afternoon.

Investigation findings
- No unauthorised logins or unusual network activity were found on any system.
- A change to the statement job on 1 October introduced a sorting error. For a batch of statements, the member's email address was matched to the next member's statement in the list.
- 347 statements were sent to the wrong member. Each misdirected statement contained the member's name, address, account number and transactions for September. No passwords or card numbers were included.
- The job was stopped at 9:35am. The remaining 11,200 statements in the run had not yet been sent.

Notifications
Because the statements contain financial information, we have assessed this as an eligible data breach and notified the privacy regulator on 3 October. All 347 affected members were contacted by phone by 6 October, and members who received someone else's statement were asked to delete it.

Actions
1. Roll back the change and add a check that the email address and statement account match before sending (complete).
2. Require a second reviewer for changes to member communication jobs (from 13 October).
3. Update the incident communications guide so early messages to staff don't speculate about causes (Owner: Communications, due 31 October).
4. Offer affected members free credit monitoring for 12 months (in progress).

Statements for the remaining members will be sent on 9 October.

From: Dr Marcus Hale <m.hale@ironbarklabs.example.com.au>
To: Product Leadership
Subject: Results - customer onboarding pilot (Sydney vs Perth)

Hi all,

Here are the results from the onboarding pilot we ran in August and September. Short version: it's mixed, and I'd caution against rolling it out nationally yet.

What we tested
New business customers in Sydney got the new guided onboarding (a 45-minute video call with a specialist in week one). Perth customers got the existing email-only onboarding. We compared the two groups on how many customers were still active after 30 days.

Headline numbers
- Sydney (guided): 412 new customers, 30-day active rate 81 per cent
- Perth (email-only): 388 new customers, 30-day active rate 74 per cent

So on the face of it, guided onboarding lifted retention by 7 percentage points.

But
The two cities weren't comparable. Sydney's sales team ran a promotion in August that gave the first month free, and 60 per cent of Sydney's new customers came through that promotion. Free-month customers usually stay active for at least 30 days because they haven't paid yet. When we look only at customers who paid from day one, the gap shrinks to 2 percentage points (78 per cent vs 76 per cent), which is within the normal month-to-month variation.

Kirsten in sales has been telling people the pilot "proved guided onboarding works", and I understand why, but the data doesn't support that yet.

Cost
Each guided session costs about $95 in specialist time. Across all new customers nationally, that's roughly $410,000 a year.

What I'd suggest
Run a proper test where customers in the same city are randomly assigned to guided or email-only, for at least 60 days. I've drafted a plan and can start in November if we agree at the 21 October leadership meeting.

Happy to walk anyone through the numbers.

Marcus
reference: Key points: onboarding pilot compared guided video onboarding (Sydney) with email-only (Perth); headline 81% vs 74% 30-day active looks like +7 points; but a Sydney free-month promotion skewed results - for paying customers only the gap is 2 points (78% vs 76%), within normal variation; national rollout would cost about $410,000 a year; Marcus recommends a randomised 60-day test, decision at 21 October meeting. TRAP: the 7-point headline and Kirsten's "proved it works" claim are not the finding - a summary saying guided onboarding improved retention by 7 points is wrong.

At the end of September, 84 staff had more than eight weeks of annual leave banked, and the total value of leave owed across the business was $3.9 million. High balances are a cost risk for the business, and people who don't take leave are more likely to burn out.

From 1 December, staff with more than eight weeks (40 days for full-time staff) of annual leave will need to agree a plan with their manager to reduce their balance. Staff will be able to cash out up to two weeks of annual leave once a year, as long as at least four weeks remain after the cash-out. This must be agreed in writing. Previously, cashing out was not allowed.

The business will close from 24 December to 2 January. Staff will need to use annual leave for the four working days in that period that are not public holidays. Staff without enough leave can take leave without pay or make up the time with their manager's agreement.

Research Summary: Voice-directed picking vs handheld scanners
Logistics Productivity Lab (fictional), Monash Valley Institute of Technology
Prepared for industry partners, October 2026

Question
Does voice-directed picking (workers wear a headset that reads out the next item and location) increase picking speed and accuracy compared with handheld scanners?

Setting
We ran the trial over ten weeks in two distribution centres in western Sydney, owned by a single grocery wholesaler. In each centre, two shifts used voice picking and two used handheld scanners. Shifts were swapped halfway through so each worker used both methods.

Participants
118 pickers took part. Thirty-one had less than six months' experience.

Results
Speed: voice picking increased lines picked per hour from an average of 142 to 156, an increase of about 10 per cent. Most of the gain came in the first four weeks after workers switched, and it stayed stable after that.

Accuracy: picking error rates fell from 0.62 per cent of lines to 0.41 per cent. In the second centre, which already had low error rates, the difference was smaller.

New workers: workers with less than six months' experience improved most, with speed up 17 per cent.

Worker feedback: in an anonymous survey, 64 per cent of pickers preferred voice picking. The most common complaint was that headsets became uncomfortable in the summer heat, and some workers said they missed being able to talk to colleagues.

Costs
Setting up voice picking for a centre of this size (about 60 pickers) cost around $210,000, including headsets, software and training. Based on wage costs, the partner estimates it would pay back in about 14 months.

Conclusion
Voice-directed picking improved both speed and accuracy, with the biggest gains among newer staff. Organisations considering the change should plan for headset comfort in hot conditions.

Limitations
Both centres belong to the same company and handle groceries. Results may differ for other product types.
reference: Key points: ten-week trial with 118 pickers in two western Sydney centres, crossover design; voice picking raised lines per hour by about 10% (142 to 156) and cut errors from 0.62% to 0.41%; newer workers gained most (speed +17%); 64% preferred it, though headsets were hot and isolating; about $210,000 per centre, payback around 14 months; limited to groceries in one company. No trap.

Riverbend Council scraps library late fees, with one exception

Riverbend City Council will stop charging late fees on overdue library books from 1 December, joining a growing number of councils across Victoria.

Councillors voted 7-2 on Tuesday night to remove overdue fines on all books, magazines and DVDs at the city's five libraries. The council will also wipe all existing overdue fines from library accounts, which currently total about $38,000 across 6,400 members.

Library services manager Ophelia Grant said fines had become a barrier for many families. "We had hundreds of children whose cards were blocked because of a few dollars in fines, and they simply stopped coming," she said. "When other councils dropped fines, they saw more books come back, not fewer."

The change does not apply to lost or damaged items. Members will still be charged the replacement cost if an item is not returned within 60 days of its due date, and their account will be blocked until the item is returned or paid for. Items borrowed through the inter-library loan service from other councils will also keep their current late fees, because those fees are set by the lending library.

Councillor Neil Ashcroft, who voted against the change, said the council was "giving up revenue at a time when rates are under pressure". The fines brought in about $52,000 last financial year, though council officers said around $19,000 of that was spent on staff time chasing payments.

Members will receive an email in November explaining the change. Those with blocked cards due only to overdue fines will have their cards unblocked automatically on 1 December.

The council will review the policy in 12 months, looking at return rates, membership numbers and the number of lost items.

Local mother of three Jade Whitfield said her family had stopped using the library after racking up $27 in fines. "We'll be back the first week," she said.

Study Write-up: Water bottles in exams and student performance
Riverstone Education Research Group (fictional), summary for school principals

Background
Some schools allow students to bring a clear water bottle into exams; others don't. A widely shared overseas study claimed that students who drank water during exams scored up to 10 per cent higher. We wanted to see whether this held up in Australian secondary schools.

What we did
We worked with 11 public secondary schools in regional New South Wales during the 2025 Year 10 half-yearly exams. In six schools, students were allowed water bottles in all exams. In five schools, students were not. We compared students' exam results with their results from the previous year, to account for differences in ability between schools.

Total students: 1,622.

What we found
Students in the water-bottle schools improved their results by an average of 1.8 marks out of 100 compared with the previous year. Students in the no-water-bottle schools improved by 1.1 marks. The difference of 0.7 marks was not statistically significant.

We did not find the 10 per cent effect reported overseas. Our result is much smaller and could be due to chance.

In a short survey after the exams, 71 per cent of students in the water-bottle schools said having water helped them concentrate, and teachers said students seemed calmer.

There were no reports of problems with water bottles, such as spills on papers or notes hidden in labels, after schools required clear bottles with labels removed.

What this means for schools
Allowing water in exams costs nothing, causes few problems and students like it. But schools shouldn't expect it to make a noticeable difference to results. Decisions should be based on student comfort and wellbeing rather than on claims about higher marks.

Limitations
Schools were not randomly allocated. The hot weather in the exam period in some regions may have affected results.

Contact: Dr Simon Achebe, Lead Researcher.
reference: Key points: 11 NSW regional schools, 1,622 Year 10 students; water-bottle schools improved 1.8 marks vs 1.1 elsewhere - a 0.7-mark difference that was not statistically significant; no sign of the overseas 10% effect; students liked it (71% said it helped concentration) and there were no problems with clear, unlabelled bottles; schools should allow it for comfort, not expected marks; schools weren't randomised. TRAP: the overseas 10% claim and student opinions are not the finding - a summary saying water improves marks is wrong.
